prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B018 as a single-part prize with the same three names. Having read the full exchange, my reasons have not changed but have become sharper. The mandate asks for an original experiment that nature has verified. Here Kane and Mele predicted a new class of insulator with protected helical edge channels, and the Molenkamp group, using HgTe/CdTe quantum wells, observed the edge-dominated conductance in 2007. Since then transport, ARPES and STM across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi-based materials have confirmed the picture, so maturity is not in question. It also opened a door: a state of matter that no one could see before, which can now be probed with instruments in many laboratories. The convergence of six members from different fields reassures me, but I do not count it as merit. What matters is that, after the round-1 exchange, nobody has produced a scientific objection that the B018 case cannot answer, while the objections to B041 (overlap with 2005 and 2012, performance versus concept) are real and unresolved.
statement.case_against: The credit gap remains the weak point and I will not minimise it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang told the experimentalists which material to grow, Zhang is deceased, and the 3D work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hsieh and Hasan) lies outside the trio. I also accept the objection from Mehlig and the chair that the 2016 prize for topological phases may be read as already covering the conceptual ground. My answer is that the 2016 prize rewarded topological order in 1D and 2D quantum Hall and spin-chain systems, whereas B018 is a time-reversal-invariant, spin-orbit-driven state in ordinary band insulators, with no magnetic field, and its experimental discovery was a separate event. Still, that is my judgement and I recall the history from memory, so the committee should check the primary papers. Practical benefit remains prospective, so the case rests on understanding of nature.

responses.point: Mehlig and the chair ask whether B018 is a distinct discovery or a refinement of the topological ideas recognised in 2016, and whether the HgTe experiment is independent or merely a realisation of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.
responses.response: On the 2016 question I think the distinction is clear enough to defend. The Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz prize rested on integer quantum Hall physics, the Haldane model with broken time-reversal symmetry, and defect-mediated phase transitions. Kane and Mele showed that a time-reversal-symmetric system with spin-orbit coupling carries a Z2 invariant, which is a different symmetry class with its own protected edge and no magnetic field, and Molenkamp's quantum wells were its first observation. On independence, the BHZ proposal selected the HgTe thickness window, but an experiment is credited for seeing the phenomenon and not for choosing the sample. The quantised edge transport could have failed, and the measurement was demanding. I would therefore keep Molenkamp in, and keep the citation tied to the prediction of the state and its first observation.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the committee can defend a citation that omits BHZ and the 3D topological insulators, and suggests experts check the primary papers on whether BHZ was the decisive step for HgTe.
responses.response: I agree that checking is worthwhile, and I would put the sequence on the record: Kane-Mele (2005) predicted the state in graphene, BHZ (2006) identified a realistic platform in HgTe, and Konig et al. (2007) observed it. The BHZ step was a platform proposal and not a new class of phase, which is why I think the trio is defensible, though I admit it is the most vulnerable point. I would also not widen the wording to 3D materials, since that would invite a claim for Fu, Moore, Hasan and others that three names cannot carry. A narrow citation that names HgTe quantum wells is more honest than a broad one that implicitly claims to cover everything. I would record in the committee minutes that the omissions are deliberate.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B041 for its clean two-name credit and reproduced 1e-18 performance, and asks whether any evidence would move the B041 supporters.
responses.response: I respect that case, and B041 is my first alternative because it is a real tool that opens a door. But the question you raise yourself, whether it is a second-generation improvement after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, is the one that makes me hesitate to put it first. The discovery must be the original experiment, and Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is original while the 1e-18 performance is a later, better realisation. A citation that rests on the lattice concept would be defensible, but the redefinition of the second has not yet happened and the fundamental-physics output is so far null results. I would be glad to revisit it in a few years. What would move me is a settled priority record among Katori, Ye, and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, and a citation that does not read as a performance prize.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B041 first, concedes that B018 has the broadest support and larger footprint, and says the clock case must rest on new capability, not on a new phase of matter.
responses.response: Thank you for stating it so directly. I agree that capability can be a legitimate ground for a physics prize, and I said as much in 2023 about attosecond physics. My difficulty is the line between a new capability and an improvement in an area already recognised twice, and you identify the same difficulty yourself with Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow and Hinkley. For B018 the new thing is a state of matter, and the original experiment can be named. I would not oppose B041 at a later date if the committee finds the topological credit too fragmented, but I do not find the credit problem for B041 smaller than for B018, only different.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from kilonovae to B018, but warns that a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators could look like an arbitrary line, and says B041 is cleaner if the topological credit is too fragmented.
responses.response: I take the arbitrariness concern seriously, but I think the line is not arbitrary: it follows the prediction of a new symmetry class and its first experimental observation, which is how the prize has usually drawn credit. Fragmentation is a feature of any mature field, and B041 also has parallel groups. I would prefer to accept that three names cannot cover every contributor and say so in the record than to switch to a candidate whose novelty is in dispute. If the committee wants robustness against criticism, the best protection is an exact and modest citation, which is why I want the HgTe quantum wells named.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, after checking the primary papers, finds that the BHZ proposal was decisive enough that omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang makes the credit unfair.
Whether the 2016 prize is judged to leave room for B018. I argue that it does, but this is a judgement on which condensed-matter members differ in weight from others.
My recollection of the dates and priority sequence (2005, 2006, 2007) comes from memory and has not been checked against the papers.
For B041, how the priority between Katori and Ye and the other groups would resolve, which I cannot judge from the materials available.
Whether the imperfect quantisation in longer HgTe edges weakens the claim that the original experiment is the decisive verification.
statement.conflict_note: I report no conflict with Kane, Mele or Molenkamp or with the alternatives B041 and B030; I have no collaboration with any credited person. I note that I share the Gothenburg environment with Johansson (Chalmers) and Mehlig (GU), as already disclosed. Johansson has disclosed ties to circuit QED (B020) and Kroll to the Chalmers quantum community; neither bears on my preferred configuration. My own field of electron microscopy is not close to any shortlisted candidate, so I rely on colleagues for atomic and astrophysics cases.
